questions.subject: Speaking
questions.learningObjective: Respond spontaneously to campus interview questions with relevant and coherent spoken elaboration.
questions.prompt: Describe an object you remember seeing at a school display. What detail stayed with you?
questions.answer: I remember a hand-drawn street map. Someone had marked the houses that shared a courtyard, which made the drawing feel like a record of daily life.
questions.explanation: Illustrative spoken response. Other relevant responses can earn credit. Recall an object and identify a concrete remembered detail.

markingGuide.description: Recall an object and identify a concrete remembered detail.
Develop the response with a relevant reason, example or detail.
Organise ideas coherently and use language that conveys the intended meaning.
Speak intelligibly with a pace that lets the listener follow.

questions.prompt: Why might a short caption help a visitor understand a display? Give an example.
questions.answer: A short caption can point out a detail that is easy to miss. Next to an old photograph, it might explain why a mark on a doorway mattered to people who lived there.

questions.prompt: How would a display arranged by date differ from one arranged by theme for visitors?
questions.answer: A date order helps visitors follow how things changed. A theme can bring objects from different periods together and make a connection easier to see. Each arrangement answers a different kind of question.
questions.explanation: Illustrative spoken response. Other relevant responses can earn credit. Distinguish the effects of two ways of organising information.

questions.subject: Speaking
questions.learningObjective: Respond spontaneously to campus interview questions with relevant and coherent spoken elaboration.
questions.prompt: A small exhibition can afford either better lighting or longer opening hours. Which should it choose if most visitors arrive after lectures? Explain your decision.
questions.answer: I would first check whether visitors can already see the displays clearly. If they can, I would extend the hours so people whose lectures end late can visit. If the lighting makes labels unreadable, that would take priority.

questions.prompt: Why might two student groups need different kinds of rehearsal space? Give an example.

questions.prompt: Your group’s rehearsal room is suddenly unavailable. How would you use the next twenty minutes productively?

questions.prompt: A college could assign fixed weekly slots or let groups reserve rooms each week. Which system would you favour if groups prepare for events on different dates?
questions.answer: I would favour weekly reservations because demand changes before events. I would keep a limit on how many slots a group can reserve so regular rehearsals are still possible.

questions.subject: Speaking
questions.learningObjective: Respond spontaneously to campus interview questions with relevant and coherent spoken elaboration.
questions.prompt: Design a simple system for sharing one rehearsal room among several groups with conflicting requests. Explain how it would handle a cancellation.
questions.answer: I would ask groups to submit two preferred times. A rotating order would decide who gets first choice each week. If a group cancels, its slot would go to the first group on a waiting list that can use it.
